page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The statement
lines: Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases,
at the same temperature and pressure, contain
steps.why: The law says the COUNT of gas molecules fixes the volume, whatever the gas — which is why one mole of any gas occupies the same 22.4 L at STP.
common_mistakes: Saying equal MASSES instead of equal volumes. Equal volumes hold equal numbers, not equal masses.
Leaving out at the same temperature and pressure.
steps.memory_tip: Count, not kind: the number of molecules sets the volume; the identity of the gas does not.
steps.margin_note: Equal volumes, same T and P, equal numbers — three pieces, one sentence.

steps.label: The mathematical form

lines.text: V ∝ n  (at constant T and P)

lines: This law gives the n in PV = nRT, and it is why
one mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 L.
steps.why: Volume proportional to moles is the symbol form of equal volumes hold equal numbers. It supplies the amount variable that completes the ideal gas equation.
common_mistakes: Writing V ∝ 1/n. More gas takes MORE room — the proportion is direct.
steps.memory_tip: Boyle gave P, Charles gave T, Avogadro gave n — the three inputs of PV = nRT.
steps.margin_note: The 22.4 L line ties this law to the gram molar volume question of the same chapter; that 22.4 L is at the older STP of 0 °C and 1 atm (at 0 °C and 1 bar the value is 22.7 L).
